cues.text: A Soldier's Wound
Born in 1491 at the castle of Loyola in the Basque province of Guipúzcoa, Íñigo López de Loyola was the youngest of thirteen children.
He was raised for a courtier's and soldier's life, proud, vain, and, by his own later admission, given to duels and romantic conquests.
He served in the household of a Castilian nobleman and then as a soldier in the armies of the Duke of Nájera.
At the siege of Pamplona in 1521 , a cannonball shattered his right leg, ending his military career and forcing months of painful convalescence at the family castle.
Denied the chivalric romances he asked for, he was given instead a life of Christ and a book of saints' lives — reading that slowly and unexpectedly reoriented his entire ambition.
Conversion at Manresa
Ignatius resolved to abandon his old life and imitate the saints he had read about.
After a night-long vigil at the shrine of Montserrat, he laid down his sword before an image of the Virgin.
He then withdrew to the town of Manresa , where he spent nearly a year in intense prayer, penance, and periods of severe spiritual desolation and consolation.
Out of this crucible came the core of his Spiritual Exercises , a structured, month-long program of meditations and prayer.
It was designed to help a retreatant discern God's will and would become one of the most influential texts in Catholic spirituality, still used in retreats worldwide.
Studies and the Gathering of Companions

Convinced that learning was necessary for the work God had in mind for him, Ignatius, already in his thirties, returned to school alongside boys half his age, eventually earning a master's degree at the University of Paris in 1534.
There he gathered a small circle of fellow students, including the young Basque nobleman Francis Xavier , whom he pursued for years before winning him over.
On 15 August 1534, Ignatius and six companions vowed poverty, chastity, and a pilgrimage to Jerusalem in a chapel at Montmartre.
When war made the pilgrimage impossible, the group instead placed itself at the disposal of the pope, and in 1540 Paul III formally approved their new religious order.
Founding the Society of Jesus

As first Superior General of the Society of Jesus , Ignatius governed the rapidly growing order from Rome for the rest of his life, drafting its Constitutions, founding schools, and directing missionaries to India, Japan, Brazil, and beyond.

He insisted on rigorous intellectual formation for Jesuits and on total, disciplined obedience to superiors and to the pope, famously summarized in his ideal of seeing all things "for the greater glory of God" — Ad Maiorem Dei Gloriam .
By the time of his death the Society numbered roughly a thousand members across Europe, Asia, and the Americas, an extraordinary expansion in barely two decades.
Legacy
Ignatius died in Rome on 31 July 1556 , worn down by decades of relentless administrative and spiritual labor.
He was canonized in 1622 alongside Francis Xavier , and his feast is kept on the day of his death.
The Society of Jesus he founded became one of the most consequential religious orders in Catholic history.

It shaped education, missions, and theology across five centuries, while his Spiritual Exercises continue to be prayed by Catholics and non-Catholics alike as a foundational tool of discernment and spiritual direction.
